Daniel is circling a real phenomenon, but the key weakness is a category-mixup: what he describes is less “empathy” being reduced by expertise than *perspective-taking being distorted by it*. The marketing and finance examples hinge on an expert confusing their own trained priors (discount rates, base rates, expected value) with the audience’s lived decision rules (salience, fantasy, narrative). That’s the classic [curse of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_knowledge): once you know how to compute something, it becomes hard to remember what it felt like not to know it. But that doesn’t imply experts are “resistant to cognitive biases” (often they’re just biased in more sophisticated ways, including overconfidence and motivated reasoning), nor does it imply they can’t understand the public; it implies they have to *work* to reconstruct the other person’s frame rather than assume “people are like me,” which is exactly the assumption Daniel warns against.

The psychotherapy example exposes an even sharper blind spot: the gap isn’t only cognitive, it’s also *normative*. If a therapist re-describes a patient’s problem through a model, the central question becomes: when is that reframing clarifying, and when is it colonizing—substituting professional categories for the patient’s own meanings? That tension is old in medicine and social science: “understanding” can become a power move unless paired with epistemic humility and feedback loops that check whether the model is helping. Daniel’s lottery reaction is a good illustration of why this matters in public life: if experts treat non-expert preferences as mere error, they may miss not just prediction (“people will buy tickets”) but the ethical dimension (when does selling hope become exploitation?). Kahneman’s split between intuitive and deliberative thinking in [*Thinking, Fast and Slow*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow) is useful here—not to sneer at intuition, but to notice that expertise often trains System 2 while markets and politics routinely monetize System 1.
